title: Do the best jazz musicians read music?
summary: Why the nonreading myth does not hold for Louis or Bunk, and Bunk's advice to start with solfege.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: Of course, there's a popular, of course, there's also the assumption that the jazz musician is better who can't read.
That he improvises better or something like that. I don't...

You'd have a hard time making that argument stick, though, too, with a person like Louis, who learned to read very well, I guess, in the 20s on the boat, and then even took lessons in Chicago. And, of course, Bunk always could probably read quite well ever since he started. In fact, that's the way Bunk advised us starting in music. First in the solfège, as they call it, the old European classical sight reading and ear training, where you have to learn to sing the melodies just by looking at them without playing anything, just be able to look at the music and hear it in your mind. And the second point was learn to pass air through your instrument, learn how to blow it in order to get a good tone and breathe easily and all. But anyway, Bunk would have had him probably working on just ear training and reading music there for a few months before they would start. In practice, I don't think he did that because any kid that comes to him, he would start them on an instrument probably in order to keep their interest. He talked about when Louis first would follow him in parades and ask Bunk to help him with some numbers. He said he asked, Louis, do you want to learn, you know, like, I forget the words you use, like the regular trumpet to learn to read or just to play Take It Away and one or two other tunes he mentioned. He said, Louis, learn Take It Away, you know, that was the Funky Butt, Funky Butt, Take It Away, and a couple of the other tunes. So any normal kid just wants to learn to play a tune, you know. But a lot of the people did actually go through that formal training, especially some of the clarinetists, anybody that studied for the T.O.'s would have had to have done that, probably learned the solfege first before they'd even get their instrument. Some of the guys will even tell you, I've talked to some of the musicians that actually had to learn the reading before they could even pick up their instrument. So evidently, it didn't really hurt some of those guys, and yet, a lot of them, as I say, you could argue either way, I think. It doesn't, if a fellow's really got the music in him and the originality, like, say, Louis had, the reading certainly didn't, didn't hurt him or destroy any originality. And it didn't, as far as we know, hurt Jelly either, too. He never played a piece, he was one person that hardly ever played anything the same way, even the pieces he recorded several times. More than most people, he'd never gotten any ruts. Probably when he started, he couldn't play either, according to several interviews that we've had. People like Mineta has said that. Said what? That Jelly couldn't read at first. He was, that he was, played on the black keys, in the key of D flat, I think was the only key he could play in at first. But somehow he learned to read quite well. Oh, Lovie Austin tells in Chicago, too, that she had to notate some of Jelly's pieces. That would be in, say, early 1920s, probably. But he finally got, he got about 46 manuscripts here that prove that he can read and write pretty well. Yet, Pops Foster told that very dumb story that Jelly couldn't read and that he couldn't even, didn't have any good left hand. They had to have another pianist on some of the records to play the left hand part. I mean, Pops must have known that better. Known better than that. In fact, Pops Foster, in one of the interviews, talks about Jelly he couldn't read. The interview with me on talking about Jelly, that he mentions that they had to get people like Clarence Williams, at least in later days, to write down the tunes and James P. Johnson in New York would write down a lot of tunes for a lot of the musicians because he was quite a trained musician too. And yet, before the interview is over, Pops talks about the job they had out at the, sorry, I got this bad throat, the job they got out on the Long Island during the World's Fair, the 1939 World's Fair. and he was in the band that only lasted about one night because Jelly talked himself out of the job too much. But he talks also about Jelly having made some arrangements for the band. So in the same breath, almost, he talks that Jelly couldn't read and he wrote out all these arrangements, which is a funny thing for a guy to do that couldn't read. But I do have all these, about 20 orchestrations that Jelly wrote out all the parts in his own hand. So we know he was a very good reader. and it didn't hurt his originality either.
